# Preface: How to Use This Book {.unnumbered epub:type=preface}



Change one number in a dataset, and how many documents are now wrong? If the number was
copied by hand into a report, a slide, an email and a web page, nobody knows without
searching. This book teaches a way of publishing with nothing to search for: you write once,
in plain text, and a web page, a Word document, a PDF, slides, an e-book, a website, a blog
and a dashboard all rebuild from that one source with one command. The program that rebuilds
them is Quarto, which is free and open source.

## Prompt, Check, Publish {.unnumbered}

The title names the method, a loop you run at every step of both projects. You **prompt** a
*coding assistant*, a program that writes files and runs commands at your request, describing
one small piece of work with its files and columns named. You **check** what it did: read
what changed, look at the result, compare it with the data. An assistant can be fluent, fast
and wrong, so this step is never skipped, and it is always yours. Then Quarto **publishes**,
rebuilding every output from the checked source the same way every time. Chapter 1 explains
why the last step can be trusted, and Chapter 2 how to make the first two reliable.

## Who this book is for {.unnumbered}

Researchers, analysts, students and anyone else who writes documents from data and is new to
Quarto, to coding assistants or to both. No programming is assumed: the book explains the
Python the assistant writes, but you do not have to write it. If the terminal is new to you,
Chapter 3 teaches the little you need, one checked step at a time.

You will need a computer on which you can install software (Windows, Mac or Linux), a free
GitHub account, and an account with one coding assistant (@sec-before-setup lists what each
needs).

## The two running examples {.unnumbered}

Every concept is tied to one of two projects, both built on real, cited data.

**A London visitor guide** (Part II). For the city's tourism office, you write one guide that
becomes a web page, a Word brief for partners, a printed flyer, a dashboard for managers and
a published website. Every visitor number in it, from the 7\,116\,929 visits to the
Natural History Museum \(South Kensington\) in 2025 down, is computed from the counts published by
the Association of Leading Visitor Attractions.

**Drinking-water risk in Colombian municipalities** (Part III). You group Colombia's
municipal zones into kinds by water safety, services and context, from 2016
to 2023, compare health and education outcomes between the kinds, and
publish the analysis as a report, slides, a blog post and a website, all from one analysis
script. Most of the data are Colombian open data, joined by official municipality codes;
rainfall comes from CHIRPS and altitude from NASA's SRTM (@sec-sources).

## How the book is organised {.unnumbered}

**Part I** covers what you need first: what Quarto does (@sec-quarto), how to work with a
coding assistant safely (@sec-assistant) and how to set up your computer (@sec-setup).
**Parts II and III** build the two projects, with the statistics explained on the way, and
each ends by changing an input and explaining what the rebuild changed. The appendices hold
the Windows setup, a cheatsheet, troubleshooting, every checkpoint, the data sources and how
this book is built.

## What a hands-on step looks like {.unnumbered #how-the-hands-on-parts-work}

Each step is a three-part box, explained in @sec-boxes: the exact prompt to give your
assistant, what it will probably run, and the few things only you can do. Prompts are
examples, not transcripts: assistants vary, so check the result rather than the wording. Four
kinds of aside step out of the main text; here is one of each.

::: why
A number computed from the data cannot disagree with the data. Asides like this one explain
the mechanism behind a step, so that you can adapt it to your own project.
:::

::: pitfall
A render started while a live preview is rendering the same file collides with it. Asides
like this one describe failures seen in practice, and how to avoid them.
:::

::: practice
**Pause and think.** The assistant reports a render with no errors. Is the work checked?

Not yet: a clean render proves that the code ran, not that its numbers are right. Asides like
this one hold judgement calls, habits and questions to pause on.
:::

::: tryit
Asides like this one are exercises. Think of one document you produce more than once, and
note where each of its numbers comes from.

::: done
you can say which of its numbers are typed by hand and which come from a file.
:::
:::

Steps marked *optional* are for readers who are ahead; nothing later depends on them.

## Two ways through {.unnumbered}

**Self-paced.** Read in order. Chapters 2 and 3 can be read and done in one sitting before
Part II; each later chapter ends at a checkpoint, where you can stop and resume later.

**Workshop-paced.** The book grew out of a six-hour workshop and keeps its shape, while
explaining what the workshop only had time to show: why each step works, where it fails, and
when not to take it. @sec-workshop has the day's agenda and the chapters each block covers
(@tbl-agenda).

## When you get stuck {.unnumbered #when-you-fall-behind}

You will get stuck: an install fails, a prompt goes wrong, a render stops with an error you
have never seen. That is expected, and the book is built for it. Every hands-on block ends at
a *checkpoint*, a folder in the workshop repository (`checkpoints/`) holding the project as it
should be at that point, with a README listing the steps to catch up. The rule is simple:
**stuck for two minutes, catch up**, and rejoin at the next block. Each exercise ends with
its catch-up line, which you paste into your assistant (@fig-catch-up).

![Catching up from a checkpoint. Your work is backed up first, so nothing is lost.](media/diagrams/catch-up){#fig-catch-up .on-light fig-alt="Stuck for two minutes, you paste the line Catch me up: follow ../quarto-workshop/checkpoints/NN/README.md into the assistant. It follows four steps. One, back up your project folder, all but its .venv environment, to a new time-stamped folder beside it. Two, copy the checkpoint in, and for the water project the data if they are missing. Three, render and check a named output. Four, rejoin at the next hands-on block, which the README names."}

A checkpoint holds the end of its block, so it can be ahead of the step you were on: after
catching up, skip the block's remaining prompts and read on to the next exercise.
@sec-checkpoints lists every checkpoint.

## Two editions {.unnumbered}

This book comes as an e-book (EPUB) and as a website, built from the same source: it is its
own first example of the method. The [website edition](https://project-delphi.github.io/quarto-workshop/book/)
runs everything interactive: three
3-D scenes and two data explorers. The e-book shows each as an animation or a still, with a
link and a QR code to the live version. Readers that cannot play animations show the first
frame, designed as a useful still, and the website respects your reduced-motion setting.

## Versions and dates {.unnumbered}

The book was built and checked with Quarto 1.10.20 (with its bundled Typst 0.15), Python 3.12
and uv, in November 2026. Facts that change, such as a model's price, an assistant's screens
or a free hosting plan's limits, carry the date they were checked, as in "(checked
2026-11-06)". Some will have changed by the time you read them; the principles around them
should not have.
